headline: Picnic notes, Grandma's old school and a sudden storm
teaser: What food is Class 8B taking to the picnic, what was school like sixty years ago, and where did Aisha and Omar hide from the rain?

articles.title: Our Class Picnic
articles.dek: Class 8B is planning a picnic in the park. Read the notes and messages about the food!
paras: It's the end of term, and Class 8B is planning a picnic in Riverside Park this Saturday. This week, lots of notes and messages went around the school, the students' homes and the class chat. Here are some of them.

NOTICE. CLASS 8B PICNIC. This Saturday, 12:00 to 3:00, in Riverside Park. Please bring some food or drink to share with the class. You don't need to bring any plates or cups. The school has got a lot of them. Please don't bring much chocolate or many sweets. Let's have a healthy picnic! Mr Hassan, Class Teacher

TEXT MESSAGE. Hi Tom! I'm making sandwiches for the picnic. Have we got any cheese at home? I need some bread too. How much bread is there in the kitchen? Please check before Mum goes to the shop. Thanks! Nadia

NOTE ON THE FRIDGE. Dad, can you buy some apples and a lot of grapes for my class picnic, please? We haven't got any juice, so please get two big bottles. Don't buy any milk. There's a lot in the fridge. Thank you! Kofi

SCHOOL CAFÉ. Fresh fruit salad: £1.50. Sorry, we haven't got many cakes today. There isn't any orange juice left, but there is some lemonade. Picnic boxes for Saturday: please order here before Thursday.

CLASS 8B CHAT. Lily: How many people are coming on Saturday? I'm making some rice salad, and I don't want to make too much. Ben: About twenty-five, I think. Lily: OK, then I'll make a lot! Ben: I can bring some water. How many bottles do we need?
MESSAGE FROM MR HASSAN. Good news! It's going to be sunny on Saturday. Please wear a hat and bring a lot of water. Have you got any questions? Come and see me in Room 12.

grammar.point: Countable, uncountable: some, any, much, many
grammar.rule: Countable nouns have a plural (apples, cups). Uncountable nouns don't (bread, milk, water). Use some in positive sentences and any in negatives and questions. Use many with countable nouns and much with uncountable nouns, usually in negatives and questions. A lot of goes with both.

articles.title: When Grandma Was at School
articles.dek: Daniel asks his grandma about her school days about sixty years ago.
paras: For our school magazine this month, Daniel Novak, 13, talked to his grandmother, Eva. She is seventy-one now. She was a student in a small town in the Czech Republic about sixty years ago. Here is their interview.

Daniel: What was your school like? Eva: It was very small. There were only two classrooms and about forty children. My teacher was Mr Horak. He was strict, but he was kind too. I wasn't afraid of him.

Daniel: Were the lessons different from my lessons? Eva: Yes, they were! There weren't any computers, of course. We wrote with pens and ink, and our fingers were always blue. Maths was my favourite subject, but history was boring for me. The books were old, and there weren't many pictures in them.

Daniel: Was the school day long? Eva: Yes, it was. Lessons started at eight o'clock, and there was school on Saturday mornings too! There wasn't a school canteen. At twelve o'clock, we went home for lunch.

Daniel: Who was your best friend? Eva: Her name was Hana. We were in the same class for eight years. We were both good at sport, and we were always together. She lives in Prague now, and we still talk on the phone every week.
Daniel: Were you a good student? Eva: Ha! Not always. I was good at maths, but I wasn't very quiet in class. One morning, Hana and I were late because we were in the park. Mr Horak wasn't happy!

Daniel: Is school better now? Eva: In some ways, yes. Your classrooms are warm and bright, and you've got computers. Our classroom was cold in winter! But we were very happy there. For me, good friends are the best thing about school.

questions.q: What is the interview mainly about?
opts: Eva's school days many years ago
questions.why: Daniel asks Eva questions about her school when she was young.
optWhy: Mr Horak was Eva's teacher, but he isn't famous, and Prague is where Hana lives now.
Correct. Every question is about Eva's school life sixty years ago.

questions.q: How many classrooms were there at Eva's school?
questions.why: Eva says there were only two classrooms.
questions.evidence: There were only two classrooms and about forty children.
optWhy: The interview doesn't say four.
Forty was the number of children, not classrooms.
Correct. There were only two classrooms.

questions.q: Eva liked maths more than history.
questions.why: Maths was her favourite subject, and history was boring for her.
questions.evidence: Maths was my favourite subject, but history was boring for me.
optWhy: Correct. Maths was her favourite, and history was boring.
The interview says the opposite.
Eva tells us clearly which subject she liked.

questions.q: In paragraph 5, who does 'We' mean in 'We were in the same class for eight years'?
questions.why: Eva is talking about her best friend, Hana.
questions.evidence: We were in the same class for eight years.
optWhy: Daniel is her grandson, not her classmate.
Mr Horak was her teacher, not a student in her class.
Correct. Eva and Hana were classmates for eight years.

questions.q: How did Mr Horak feel when Eva and Hana were late?
questions.why: Eva says Mr Horak wasn't happy.
optWhy: Correct. 'Wasn't happy' means he was unhappy.
Eva wasn't afraid of him, and he wasn't afraid either.

questions.q: Eva says Mr Horak was 'strict'. What does this mean?
opts: He wanted students to follow the rules.
questions.why: A strict teacher makes students follow the rules.
questions.evidence: He was strict, but he was kind too.
optWhy: Funny is a different word. 'But he was kind too' shows strict is not always nice.
Correct. Strict means making people follow the rules.
Eva and Hana were late, not Mr Horak.

grammar.point: Past simple of be: was / were
grammar.rule: Was and were are the past of am, is and are. Use was with I, he, she and it. Use were with you, we and they. Negatives are wasn't and weren't, and in questions the verb comes first: Was it…? Were you…?

examples.text: There were only two classrooms and about forty children.
He was strict, but he was kind too.
There weren't any computers, of course.
Daniel: Were you a good student?

items.q: My grandparents ___ at home yesterday evening.
items.why: They (my grandparents) → were. Yesterday is in the past.
Your teacher = he or she, so the question starts with Was.

items.q: I ___ at school on Monday because I was ill.
items.why: I → was, so the negative is wasn't.

items.q: There ___ a lot of snow last winter.
items.why: Snow is one thing we can't count, so we use there was.

items.q: Where ___ you at eight o'clock last night?
My friends ___ late for the bus this morning.
items.why: My friends = they, so we use were.

articles.title: Caught in the Storm
articles.dek: Aisha and her little brother walk home from school, and then the sky goes dark.
paras: Last Friday, Aisha and her little brother Omar walked home from school. In the morning, the sky was blue and the sun was warm. So Aisha left her umbrella at home. That was a big mistake!

On the way home, the weather changed very quickly. Dark clouds came over the hills, and the wind started to blow. Then it began to rain. Soon the rain was very heavy, and the street turned into a river.
Suddenly, there was a loud noise. It was thunder! Omar cried and held Aisha's hand. "We need to find somewhere dry," Aisha said. She looked around and saw a small library on the corner of the street.
They ran to the library and opened the door. They were very wet, and their shoes were full of water. A kind librarian, Mrs Lee, gave them two towels. She also made hot chocolate for them.

Aisha phoned her mum and told her about the storm. "Stay there," Mum said. "I'll come in the car after work." Omar found a book about storms, and Aisha read it to him. After that, he wasn't scared any more.
An hour later, the rain stopped and the sun came out again. Mum arrived and thanked Mrs Lee. On the way to the car, Omar saw a beautiful rainbow over the park. "Look!" he shouted.
That evening, Aisha put her umbrella in her school bag. "From now on, it stays in my bag," she said. Omar laughed. "And I want to go back to that library next week!"

keySentences.text: So Aisha left her umbrella at home.
keySentences.note: The weather was good in the morning, so she didn't take her umbrella.

keySentences.text: Dark clouds came over the hills, and the wind started to blow.
keySentences.note: Came is irregular (come → came). Started is regular (start → started).

keySentences.text: She looked around and saw a small library on the corner of the street.
keySentences.note: First she looked around, then she saw the library.

keySentences.text: A kind librarian, Mrs Lee, gave them two towels.
keySentences.note: Mrs Lee helped the children get dry.

keySentences.text: An hour later, the rain stopped and the sun came out again.
keySentences.note: Time words like 'an hour later' move the story on.

questions.why: Aisha left her umbrella at home because the morning was sunny.

optWhy: The story says she left it at home, not at school.
Correct. She left it at home.

questions.q: What happened first on the way home?

There was a loud noise of thunder.
questions.why: First the clouds came, then the rain, then the thunder.
questions.evidence: Dark clouds came over the hills, and the wind started to blow.
optWhy: Correct. The clouds came before the rain.
The rain came after the clouds and the wind.

questions.q: How did Omar feel when he heard the thunder?
questions.why: Omar cried and held his sister's hand.
questions.evidence: Omar cried and held Aisha's hand.
optWhy: Crying doesn't show he was excited.
The story doesn't say he was tired.
Correct. Crying and holding her hand show he was scared.

questions.q: The library was very near the children's school.
questions.why: The library was on a street on the way home, but the story doesn't say how near the school it was.
questions.evidence: She looked around and saw a small library on the corner of the street.
optWhy: The story doesn't say it was near the school.
We can't say it is wrong, because the story gives no information.
Correct. We only know it was on the corner of the street.

questions.q: In paragraph 5, who does 'I' mean in 'I'll come in the car after work'?
questions.why: Mum is talking on the phone to Aisha.
questions.evidence: "I'll come in the car after work."
optWhy: Aisha is on the phone, but Mum says these words.
Correct. Mum is going to drive to the library after work.
Mrs Lee is in the library. She doesn't need to come.

questions.q: What is the story mainly about?
opts: two children who found a safe place in a storm
a girl who lost her umbrella at school
a librarian who teaches children about the weather
questions.why: Aisha and Omar got wet in a storm and waited in a library.
optWhy: Correct. The library was a safe, dry place in the storm.
Aisha didn't lose her umbrella. She left it at home.
Mrs Lee gave them towels and hot chocolate. She didn't teach them.

grammar.point: Past simple: regular and irregular verbs
grammar.rule: Use the past simple for finished actions in the past (last Friday, an hour later). Regular verbs add -ed: walk → walked, stop → stopped, cry → cried. Irregular verbs change in other ways, and you need to learn them: come → came, see → saw, run → ran.

She looked around and saw a small library on the corner of the street.
They ran to the library and opened the door.

items.why: Yesterday is in the past, and watch is regular: watched.
